title: SwitchFold: Code-Agnostic Succinct Polynomial Commitments via Recursive Code Switching
authors: Mingshu Cong, Tsz Hon Yuen, and Siu-Ming Yiu
abstract:
We study hash-based polynomial commitment schemes (PCSs) over large prime fields that scale to witnesses containing billions of scalars. Such PCSs are important for emerging data-science-related applications of zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs). Our goal is to reduce prover time while preserving polylogarithmic proof size and verifier time. To this end, we seek code agnostic, succinct PCS constructions that can be instantiated with any linear code over any target field, allowing the most efficient code for the chosen field to be selected.

Our SwitchFold construction achieves polylogarithmic verification by recursively applying the code-switching technique between codes of decreasing block lengths. Prior code-switching PCSs switch from an unstructured code to a foldable code; in contrast, SwitchFold requires no code foldability and thus decouples PCS design from code design. For a polynomial of size N and security parameter λ, instantiating SwitchFold with linear-time encodable codes yields O(N) prover time and O(λ log^2 N) proof size and verifier time.

We instantiate SwitchFold with the Brakedown codes (Golovnev et al., CRYPTO ’23) and the recently proposed quasi-Abelian (QA) codes (Li et al., IACR ePrint ’26), yielding BrakeFold and QAFold, respectively. At N = 2^30, QAFold achieves the fastest prover time among all evaluated PCSs with succinct verification. Compared with TensorSwitch (Bünz et al., IACR ePrint ’25), the other code-agnostic PCS, QAFold reduces total and marginal prover time by factors of 2.2× and 2.7× under the
same QA-code instantiation. With Brakedown codes, BrakeFold reduces the marginal prover time per additional opening by a factor of 2.9× relative to TensorSwitch.

1 Introduction
Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs)
enable an untrusted prover to convince a verifier, using a succinct proof with at
most polylogarithmic proof size, that an NP statement is true. Polynomial com-
mitment schemes (PCSs) are a central primitive underlying zkSNARKs; they
allow a prover to succinctly commit to a polynomial and later open the commit-
ment by proving polynomial evaluations at selected points. The eﬀiciency of the
PCS directly affects the eﬀiciency of the zkSNARK protocols.
    In this paper, we study hash-based, field-agnostic, large-scale PCS with the
goal of minimizing the prover time while maintaining polylogarithmic proof size
and verifier time. Following Brakedown [28] and BaseFold [46], we call a PCS
field-agnostic if it can be instantiated over any suﬀiciently large finite field with-
out relying on any special algebraic structure of the field. This property is partic-
ularly valuable for emerging data-science-related applications of zkSNARKs such
as zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML), which produces succinct proofs for
neural-network computations. zkML requires fixed-point numerical fidelity, for
which certain large prime fields, such as the Mersenne field F2127 −1 , are prefer-
able to mitigate unintended wraparound while retaining eﬀicient field arithmetic.
Instantiating a PCS over such fields requires the field-agnostic property. Since
modern neural networks may contain billions of parameters, the PCS must sup-
port commitments and openings at very large scale.
    By definition, zkSNARKs require proof size and verifier time to grow at most
polylogarithmically with the witness size. Subject to this succinctness require-
ment, prover time becomes the primary optimization objective. Once a PCS
achieves polylogarithmic proof size and verifier time, recursive composition can
compress its proofs to constant size by using a fast-prover PCS as the inner ar-
gument and a constant-size SNARK as the outer wrapper. For suﬀiciently large
witnesses, the cost of the outer wrapper is small relative to that of generating the
inner proof, making the prover time of the inner PCS the dominant bottleneck.
    We work in the hash-based setting: the prover encodes the polynomial coeﬀi-
cient vector or matrix with a linear code, commits to the codeword via a Merkle
tree, and answers polynomial evaluation claims by opening sampled positions
with Merkle authentication paths. This setting avoids elliptic-curve and pairing
assumptions, requires no trusted setup, and is plausibly post-quantum secure
in the random-oracle model [33,37]. By replacing the expensive group opera-
tions required by ECC-based PCSs [15,18,27,29,32,35] with field arithmetic and
hashing, hash-based schemes achieve the fastest known concrete prover times
at large scale. More recently, lattice-based PCSs have offered another promis-
ing post-quantum route [13,21], but their concrete prover eﬀiciency is not yet
competitive in this regime; we therefore focus on hash-based PCSs.
    Within the domain of hash-based PCSs, we introduce the notion of code
agnosticity: a PCS is code-agnostic if it can be instantiated with any linear code
while maintaining polylogarithmic proof size and verifier time, without relying
on special structure of the code. In such a construction, faster encoding directly
reduces prover time, while larger relative distance directly reduces proof size

and verifier time. Code agnosticity therefore decouples the design of PCSs and
zkSNARKs from the design of linear codes. It implies field agnosticity, whereas
the converse does not hold. We show that a code-agnostic PCS can be obtained
through a careful combination of several standard techniques from the zkSNARK
literature while nevertheless delivering strong concrete performance.


1.1 Our Results

In this work, we present a generic transformation, based on recursive code switch-
ing, from a sequence of linear codes with geometrically decreasing block lengths
to a hash-based multilinear PCS. If each code admits linear-time encoding in its
block length, for witness size N and security parameter λ, the resulting PCS has
O(N ) prover time and O(λ log2 N ) proof size and verifier time. Our construction
does not rely on any algebraic structure of the underlying linear codes and is
therefore code-agnostic.
    Instantiating our framework with the Brakedown code [28] and the recently
proposed quasi-Abelian (QA) codes [36] yields two concrete PCSs, which we
call BrakeFold and QAFold, respectively. Both schemes can be instantiated over
arbitrary large prime fields. Recursive code switching reduces the proof size and
verifier time of the original Brakedown- and QA-code-based PCSs from square-
root to polylogarithmic complexity while retaining their eﬀicient prover.
    For N = 230 , λ = 100, and 64 threads, the marginal prover times of BrakeFold
and QAFold are 91.1 s and 71.4 s per additional opening, while their total prover
times, including an unamortized Decide phase, are 754.4 s and 88.8 s, respec-
tively. Among the evaluated PCSs with succinct verification, QAFold achieves the
fastest prover. Relative to TensorSwitch [17], the fastest competing prover in our
evaluation, QAFold reduces marginal and total prover time by factors of 2.7×
and 2.2×, respectively, when both use the same QA code. Similarly, BrakeFold
reduces marginal prover time by 2.9× relative to its TensorSwitch counterpart.
At N = 226 , the largest instance the widely used BaseFold [46] can process within
our memory limit, BrakeFold and QAFold reduce total prover time by 2.3× and
15.4×, and proof size by 2.6× and 4.4×, respectively. The QAFold verifier is also
2.0× faster, while BrakeFold matches the BaseFold verifier time.
SwitchFold: Code-Agnostic PCS with Polylogarithmic Verification.
Our main contribution is a code-agnostic PCS construction, called SwitchFold,
based on recursive code switching. It achieves linear prover time and polyloga-
rithmic proof size and verifier time using any sequence of codes satisfying some
generic eﬀiciency conditions.

Theorem 1 (Informal; see Theorem 6). Let {Cj : Fkj → Fnj }dj=0 be a
sequence of linear codes whose block lengths satisfy kj = k0 tj for a fixed constant
t ≥ 2, where d is chosen so that kd t = N for witness size N . Assume that each Cj
admits O(kj )-time encoding and has relative distance uniformly bounded below.
Then, for security parameter λ, SwitchFold yields a multilinear PCS with O(N )
prover time and O(λ log2 N ) proof size and verifier time.


                                         3
    The eﬀiciency of SwitchFold is determined by the performance of the un-
derlying code sequence: prover time is dominated by the total encoding time
across code levels, while proof size and verifier time are governed by the rela-
tive distance. Consequently, faster encoding or larger relative distance directly
improves the resulting PCS eﬀiciency. In this sense, SwitchFold decouples PCS
design from code design. Like other hash-based PCS constructions, it is secure
in the random-oracle model and plausibly post-quantum secure.
BrakeFold and QAFold: Outperforming State-of-the-Art Succinct PCSs
in Prover Time. Our second contribution provides optimized instantiations of
the SwitchFold framework with the Brakedown [28] and QA codes [36], yield-
ing BrakeFold and QAFold, respectively. Among the PCSs with polylogarithmic
proof size and verifier time, QAFold achieves the fastest total prover time for
large witnesses. Although BrakeFold is less competitive in total prover time, its
marginal prover time per additional instance remains eﬀicient for repeated PCS
openings. Together, these results establish a new prover eﬀiciency benchmark
for hash-based PCSs.
    Both Brakedown and QA codes admit eﬀicient encoding but lack foldability,
a property traditionally used to achieve polylogarithmic openings, as in FRI-
based PCSs using Reed–Solomon (RS) codes [7] and BaseFold using random
foldable codes (RFCs) [46]. Foldability, however, typically comes at the cost of
more expensive encoding. Only recently did TensorSwitch [17] show that such
succinctness can be achieved without foldable  √ codes. Consequently, the origi-
nal Brakedown and QA-code PCSs have O( λN ) proof size and verifier time,
limiting their applicability to large instances.
    The code-switching framework of Ron-Zewi and Rothblum [39] traditionally
combines the fast encoding of a non-foldable source code with the succinctness
of a foldable target code, as demonstrated by Blaze [14] and BrakingBase [38].
These constructions, however, still rely on target-code foldability, and their code-
switching cost depends on the encoding eﬀiciency of the foldable target code. In
contrast, SwitchFold recursively switches between non-foldable codes of decreas-
ing block lengths, eliminating the need for an auxiliary foldable code. Moreover,
SwitchFold uses the accumulation scheme [16] to defer the generator-matrix
MLE claims introduced by code switching until finalization, substantially re-
ducing the marginal prover cost of each additional PCS opening.

SwitchFold uses code switching to combine fast encoding with succinct verifi-

difference is that our reduction relies on generic code switching, rather than on
foldability of the underlying codes. This makes SwitchFold code-agnostic.

1.3 Technical Overview
Fig. 1 illustrates the framework of SwitchFold, which consists of three modules:
(1) Recursive code switching reduces an MLE claim on a witness matrix com-
    mitted under a large interleaved code to an MLE claim under interleaved
    codes with progressively decreasing block lengths, ultimately yielding an
    MLE claim on a short vector. Along the way, each code switch produces an
    additional MLE claim on the corresponding generator matrix.
(2) Accumulation of generator-matrix MLE claims accumulates and defers the
    opening of generator-matrix MLE claims. Because the generator matrices
    remain fixed across witnesses, these claims can be proved together when the
    multiple PCS openings are finalized. 4
(3) Final recursive opening of generator-matrix MLE claims is performed only
    once using recursive code switching, after the generator-matrix claims aris-
    ing from multiple PCS openings have been accumulated. At each level, the
    current generator matrix is committed to under an interleaved code derived
    from the code at the next lower level. Code switching then reduces its MLE
    opening problem to a new MLE claim on the smaller generator matrix. The
    recursion terminates at the base level. 5

Recursive Code Switching for Interleaved Codes. In hash-based PCSs,
committing to a message m under a linear code C means publishing the Merkle
root of the codeword Enc[C](M ), where Enc[C] denotes the encoding function

the evaluation of the unique multilinear extension polynomial of M at a given
point. In our formulation, this MLE claim is written as a vector–matrix–vector

2.4 Oracle and PCS

We formulate polynomial commitment schemes as a special class of crypto-

message and later answers queries about that message with proofs authenticating
the responses. This formulation is convenient for recursive PCS constructions, in

4.1 Accumulating Generator-Matrix MLE Claims
Recursive code switching reduces MLE claims under one code to MLE claims
under a smaller code, while introducing additional MLE claims on the generator
matrix of the source code. In particular, Line 21 of Algorithm 1 requires proving
MLE claims for all generator matrices in the code sequence. Thus, the claimed

linear prover time relies on the assumption that each generator-matrix MLE
claim can be proved in time linear in the corresponding block length.
    This assumption of linear prover time is reasonable from an asymptotic per-
spective. If the encoding algorithm of a code with generator matrix G runs
in time linear in the block length, then the generator-matrix MLE evaluation
v = l⊤ Gr = hl, Enc[C](r)i can also be computed in linear time. When the en-
coder admits a linear-size arithmetic-circuit representation, techniques such as
R1CS [9] or Plonk [26] can express this computation as a constraint system.
However, this generic approach may incur large concrete constants. As a result,
generator-matrix MLE openings may dominate the prover cost in Algorithm 1,
offsetting the gains from recursive code switching.
    We mitigate this cost by exploiting the fact that the generator matrices
are fixed across repeated PCS openings. Suppose the same code sequence is
used to commit to multiple witness matrices M (1) , . . . , M (T ) . Although the
witnesses differ, their openings generate MLE claims to the same generator-
matrix oracles {OMLE (Gj )}dj=1 . Instead of proving these generator-matrix MLE
claims independently for each witness, we accumulate them across witnesses and
query the corresponding MLE oracle only once per code level during finalization.
    This accumulation model is well suited to many zkSNARK applications, par-
ticularly blockchain Layer-2 zk-rollups. Proofs for multiple computations within
a block may use the same code sequence, allowing the sequencer to accumulate
their generator-matrix MLE claims and prove them at block finalization with
only one opening per code level.

5 Instantiation with Concrete Linear Codes
5.1 Choosing the Right Codes
Code agnosticity gives SwitchFold the flexibility to use arbitrary linear codes.
The code sequence may even combine codes from different code families across
levels. The concrete performance of SwitchFold, however, depends directly on
the properties of the selected codes. Choosing an appropriate code sequence is
therefore essential for concrete eﬀiciency.
    The top-level code has the greatest effect on prover time. To commit to
a witness matrix M ∈ Fkd ×t , the prover computes Enc[Cdt ](M ) and Merkle-
commits to the resulting codeword. Fast encoding of the top-level code directly
reduces this dominant cost. For a fixed block length, a higher rate also produces a
shorter codeword and reduces the number of hashes required by the commitment.
    The priorities change at lower levels. Recursive opening commits to matri-
ces whose dimensions decrease geometrically, so the contribution of lower-level
encoding to total prover time is smaller. Relative distance, however, determines
the number of proximity queries at every level: a larger relative distance reduces
both proof size and verifier time. It can therefore be advantageous to use a fast-
encoding code at the top level and codes with better distance at lower levels,
even if their encoders are moderately slower.
    Moreover, the final Decide protocol depends on the arithmetization of Gj .
The reduction ΠGj represents its MLE claims using the dense matrix Hj and,
when necessary, the claim-dependent auxiliary matrix Sj . Thus, the dimensions
of these matrices and the prover and verifier costs of ΠGj determine the code-
specific cost of the final recursive opening.
    These observations give the following principles for selecting a code sequence:
 – prioritize fast encoding and a favorable rate at the top level;
 – seek a favorable rate–distance tradeoff at every level, placing greater empha-
   sis on relative distance at lower levels; and
 – prefer eﬀicient generator-matrix arithmetizations, with small Hj and Sj and
   an eﬀicient reduction ΠGj .

7 Conclusion
We proposed SwitchFold, a new hash-based PCS construction based on re-
cursive code switching. Our construction transforms a sequence of codes with
geometrically increasing block lengths, linear-time encoding, and the required
eﬀicient reductions for their generator matrices into a PCS with polylogarithmic
proof size and verifier time. It relies only on generic coding-theoretic properties,
rather than on foldability of the underlying codes. We instantiated SwitchFold
with the Brakedown and QA code sequences, obtaining BrakeFold and QAFold.
At N = 230 , QAFold requires 88.8 s of total prover time, the lowest among all
evaluated PCSs with polylogarithmic proof size and verifier time.
